question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (fraction \(VE\) fully protected with hazard 0; fraction \(1-VE\) fully susceptible with hazard \(\lambda\)), the incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is computed as total events divided by total person-time. The protected individuals contribute events = 0 but add full follow-up time \(T\) to the denominator. This inflates person-time relative to the unvaccinated arm (where rate exactly recovers \(\lambda\)), yielding IRR < \(1-VE\). Therefore \(1-\)IRR > \(VE\), i.e., the quantity overestimates the vaccine efficacy parameter. (The bias vanishes only in the limit of vanishingly small cumulative hazard.) 

A. overestimate

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fixed fraction p of recipients are fully protected (per-exposure susceptibility = 0) while the remainder have zero protection. Under a constant force of infection the vaccinated incidence rate is therefore exactly (1-p) times the unvaccinated rate, so IRR = 1-p and 1-IRR recovers p. That quantity is also the average per-exposure vaccine efficacy, hence the estimator is unbiased. (The same algebra holds for a leaky vaccine under constant hazard; the distinction between the two models appears only with time-varying hazards or with cumulative-incidence measures.)

C. correctly estimate

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The incidence rate (force of infection) among the vaccinated arm equals (1 - p)λ, where p is the fraction of individuals rendered completely immune and λ is the rate among the unvaccinated. Thus 1 - IRR recovers p exactly, which is the per-exposure efficacy of an all-or-nothing vaccine. Hence the answer is C.

(The result assumes a constant external hazard; depletion or waning would alter the numerical value but not the direction of the comparison.)

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fixed fraction p of individuals are fully protected (infection probability per exposure = 0) while the remainder (1-p) behave exactly like unvaccinated individuals. When incidence rates are computed from person-time at risk, the vaccinated-group rate is therefore exactly (1-p) times the unvaccinated rate, so IRR = 1-p and 1-IRR = p. This quantity p is also the average per-exposure efficacy (p·1 + (1-p)·0). Hence 1-IRR recovers the per-exposure efficacy exactly (assuming proper person-time denominators that avoid depletion bias). The answer is therefore C.

(The distinction between all-or-nothing and leaky vaccines appears only when cumulative incidence ratios rather than incidence-rate ratios are used; the question specifically asks about the incidence-rate ratio.)

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fixed fraction \(p\) of recipients receive complete (100%) protection and the remainder receive none. Under a constant force of infection, the vaccinated cohort therefore experiences an incidence rate exactly \((1-p)\) times that of the unvaccinated cohort at every instant. Consequently the incidence-rate ratio equals \(1-p\), and \(1-\text{IRR}\) recovers \(p\) exactly. Because the per-exposure efficacy is also \(p\) (complete protection for fraction \(p\), zero for the rest), the estimator is unbiased. (The same equality holds for leaky vaccines under constant force, but the question concerns only the all-or-nothing case.)

Thus the correct choice is C.

(The result can change once the population is closed and depletion occurs, but the canonical comparison assumes an external, constant hazard.)

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns an all-or-nothing vaccine (a random fraction VE of recipients are fully protected; the rest receive zero protection) and whether 1-IRR recovers the per-exposure efficacy parameter.  

Under a constant force of infection λ acting on susceptibles, the instantaneous IRR at t = 0 equals exactly 1 − VE. With any appreciable cumulative incidence, however, susceptibles are depleted faster in the vaccinated arm (only the unprotected fraction can be infected). Consequently the observed incidence rate in that arm falls relative to the unvaccinated arm, driving the time-averaged IRR below 1 − VE. Thus 1 − IRR systematically exceeds the true per-exposure efficacy, i.e., overestimates it.  

(The result reverses for a “leaky” vaccine, but that is outside the scope of the present question.)  

Final answer: A. overestimate

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fixed fraction \(p\) of recipients are fully protected (individual-level efficacy = 1) while the rest have zero protection. This produces a time-varying population incidence rate ratio: IRR(\(t\)) = \((1-p)\exp(p\lambda t)\), where \(\lambda\) is the force of infection. The observable (average) IRR therefore exceeds \(1-p\), so the quantity \(1-\)IRR is smaller than \(p\). Because \(p\) is precisely the per-exposure vaccine efficacy parameter in this model, \(1-\)IRR underestimates it. Hence the correct choice is B.

(The same calculation shows the opposite bias for a leaky vaccine, confirming the result is specific to the all-or-nothing mechanism.)

8.text:
